extracted.intended_audience: Authors of systematic reviews (particularly Cochrane intervention review authors) and their data-extraction teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, conducting, and checking data collection and extraction for intervention systematic reviews, including what data to collect (outcomes, harms, results), how to design forms/tools, and procedural expectations for duplicate extraction and resolving disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention integrity (implementation fidelity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect information about how completely and accurately the intervention was delivered (integrity), including whether interventions were standardized or tailored and how setting/context affected delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about integrity can help determine whether unpromising results are due to a poorly conceptualized intervention or to incomplete delivery of prescribed components; it also informs feasibility of implementation in real settings. Whether deviations from intended interventions threaten bias depends on whether the review is interested in effect of assignment versus effect of adherence. Example: process evaluation in smoking cessation in pregnancy showed variable implementation and reduced effectiveness when interventions were changed or culturally inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process evaluations (mechanisms and implementation factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, collect whether trials conducted process evaluations and measured key process factors that might influence the intervention’s effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process evaluations use flexible, mixed quantitative and qualitative methods to evaluate mechanisms between intended implementation and actual effect. Review authors should aim to collect information on whether trials accounted for or measured key process factors and whether those that addressed integrity showed greater impact. See Chapter 21 for guidance and consider process evaluations as a source of factors influencing effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes — collect five elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For each outcome, collect the five elements: (1) outcome domain/title; (2) measurement tool/instrument (including definitions, scale names, score direction, thresholds); (3) specific metric used for each participant; (4) method of aggregation; (5) timing of measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: only outcomes defined in the protocol should be described in detail; however, listing names of all outcomes measured can help assess risk of bias due to missing outcome data. Further considerations for economics and patient-reported outcomes are discussed in other chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effects (harms) data collection and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect detailed information on harms including how adverse events were collected (systematically vs non-systematically) and specific items about each reported adverse event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful items to collect: any coding system/terminology and version (e.g. MedDRA), name of adverse events, reported intensity (mild/moderate/severe), whether categorized as 'serious', whether investigators attributed event to intervention, time point (e.g. counts over study duration), methods for selecting adverse events for publication (e.g. ≥5% rule), and associated results. Be cautious: non-systematic collection underestimates frequency and heterogeneity in collection methods introduces bias; avoid synthesizing harms collected differently. Precise definitions and intensity thresholds should be recorded as they vary across studies. Absence of mention does not equal absence of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results data — restrict to protocol-specified outcomes and pre-specified selection framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect results only for intervention groups and outcomes specified in the protocol; pre-specify a framework to choose between multiple reported measures/results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols should be specific about outcome domains, measurement tools, time points, and summary statistics. Create a hierarchy of preferred measures or rules (e.g. median effect, averaging) to choose among multiple eligible results; report any changes to the framework. Record unit of analysis for each result. Be alert for unexpected important findings, especially serious adverse effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing intervention groups in multi-arm studies (MECIR C50)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a study has more than two intervention arms, include in the review only interventions that meet the eligibility criteria and clearly report that other arms were present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include irrelevant interventions. Make clear in the 'Characteristics of included studies' table that multiple arms were present when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making maximal use of available data (MECIR C47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and utilize the most detailed numerical data possible that will facilitate analyses of included studies, including alternative statistics when primary data are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 2×2 tables or means/SDs are not reported, collect effect estimates, CIs, test statistics, P values, or individual participant data where available. Derive 2×2 tables or SDs from reported statistics when possible; RevMan calculator and inverse-variance formats can help. Collect any reported numerical detail that may enable conversion to the required format for meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking accuracy of numeric data in the review (MECIR C51)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the magnitude and direction of effects reported by studies with how they are presented in the review to check for errors and inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure qualitative agreement (direction of effect and statistical significance) between original data and review presentation. Forest plot results should agree with original reports if the same effect measure and model are used. This helps detect typographical errors, data manipulation errors, and entry mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and piloting of data collection forms (MECIR C43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a structured data collection form that has been piloted and assessed for usability; forms may be paper, electronic, or part of a data system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data collection forms link review questions and eligibility criteria to extracted data, serve as provenance records, and are the source of data for analysis. Forms should be piloted, versioned, and available to the CRG on request. Consider separate forms for different purposes (e.g. eligibility assessment vs extraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting appropriate data collection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose data collection tools (paper, electronic forms, data systems) based on review size, team size, and available resources, considering advantages and disadvantages of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data systems benefit large reviews and updates, allow automation and integration with screening, linking data to report locations, monitoring progress, simultaneous entry, and export to analysis software; they may have higher resource and training needs. Paper forms require low resources but are inefficient for large teams. Consider compatibility with analytical software and RevMan imports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principles for data collection forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct easy-to-use forms that collect sufficient, unambiguous data faithfully representing the source and minimize the need to return to source documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps and tips: (1) develop outlines of expected tables/figures to decide amount of data; (2) group data elements (see Table 5.3.a); (3) frame data items optimally — ask closed-ended questions where possible, include 'other, specify', include 'not applicable','not reported','cannot tell' options, record raw data (quotes) where judgement required, record source location; (4) pilot-test forms with several people, check accuracy against source documents, include version numbers/dates, record reviewer and date, include study ID and report ID, provide definitions/instructions next to items, and leave space for notes. Revise forms as needed and consider re-extracting previously extracted reports if major changes are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design detail: framing questions to minimize subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame items to focus on what is reported rather than what was done, avoid open-ended uncoded text, and include options that capture uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ask 'Did the article report that participants were masked to the intervention?' rather than 'Were participants masked?'. Include 'cannot tell' options to flag items warranting contact with study authors. Record raw source quotations used to justify judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should extract data — required skills and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Data extractors should have basic topic understanding, knowledge of study design, data analysis and statistics, attention to detail, and training on the forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer complementary disciplines (methodologist + topic specialist). Because extraction errors are rarely detected later, multiple persons should extract data to minimize errors and bias. Training and practice with the form are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate extraction of study characteristics (MECIR C45)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (at least) two people working independently to extract study characteristics and define in advance the process for resolving disagreements (highly desirable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplication reduces mistakes and the influence of a single person’s biases. It is less critical for study characteristics than for outcome data and thus not mandatory, but recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate extraction of outcome data (MECIR C46)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (at least) two people working independently to extract outcome data and define in advance the process for resolving disagreements (mandatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate extraction reduces errors and biased selection for outcome data, which feed directly into evidence syntheses and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training data extractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide training at the start and periodically to familiarize extractors with topic, methods, the form/system, and likely issues including algorithms for conflicting locations of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pilot testing to identify ambiguous questions and agree coding instructions. Reinforce agreed algorithms when items appear in multiple report locations or sources. Blinding extractors to report authors is generally not recommended for Cochrane reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extracting data from multiple reports of the same study
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the study as the unit of interest and collate/reconcile information across multiple reports; do not discard reports without careful examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two main strategies: (a) extract from each report separately and combine forms, or (b) extract all reports directly into a single form. Choice depends on report nature. When conflicting data cannot be resolved by contacting authors, identify the 'main' data source. Use modified PRISMA-style flow diagrams to document and collate multiple reports. Be mindful that multiple reports may contain unique information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability, disagreement resolution, and audit trail
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify in the protocol how disagreements between extractors will be identified and resolved; record presence and resolution of disagreements and keep copies of 'as extracted' data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First attempt resolution by discussion; if unresolved, arbitrate with a third person or contact study authors. Maintain the original extracted data in addition to consensus data to allow assessment of coding reliability.
